newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope gets clean bill of health after appendectomy.
newsitem.headline: Pope gets clean bill of health after appendectomy.

text.p: Pope John Paul was expected to be back on his feet on Wednesday, a day after a smooth operation to remove his appendix which also failed to show any signs of more serious illness.

Doctors who carried out what was described as a "textbook appendectomy" said it showed that the Roman Catholic leader was not suffering from another tumour. But they urged the 76-year old Polish pontiff to take life more quietly in future.

"The Pope is made of strong stuff but he should work a little less," Corrado Manni, the anaesthetist at Tuesday's 50-minute operation, told reporters. "He should save himself, the years are passing even for him," he added.

It was the Pope's fourth abdominal operation since he was elected in 1978 and the sixth time he has been treated at Rome's Gemelli hospital since surgeons there saved his life after an assassination attempt in 1981.

Francesco Crucitti, chief surgeon at the hospital, told a packed news conference on Tuesday that the latest operation had been a "textbook appendectomy" and he firmly rejected widespread speculation that the Pope might be suffering from a tumour.
"Now is the moment to put a stop to these fallacies," Crucitti said. "I exclude it in the most categorical way."
Crucitti removed a growth from the Pope's intestine in 1992 that was the size of an orange and starting to turn malignant.

The Vatican's announcement last month that three bouts of fever which have afflicted the Pope since Christmas had been caused by recurrent inflammation of the appendix was met with scepticism from the media and independent doctors.

"He has never had any other growth (since 1992)," the chief surgeon said on Tuesday, adding that he expected the Pope would be able to leave his bed sometime on Wednesday and might be out of hospital in less than seven days.
The next medical bulletin was due at 1000 GMT.

However the team of doctors ducked questions about a violent trembling of the left hand which troubles the Pope. The media has speculated that the trembling, along with facial rigidity and a stooped gait, could be signs of Parkinson's disease, a debilitating neurological disorder.
"Neurology is not my specialisation," the anaesthetist Manni said, but added that people connected such trembling with a possible decline in a person's mental abilities.
"Parkinson's disease is one thing, Alzheimer's disease is another," he said. Alzheimer's is a progressive degenerative ailment that impairs memory, thinking and behaviour.

Messages of goodwill for the Pontiff poured in from around the world. The White House sent a message from President Bill Clinton conveying "the best wishes of the president for his speedy recovery", spokesman Mike McCurry said.
Poland's ex-communist prime minister, Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, said he was looking forward to the Pope's planned visit to his homeland next year.

The pontiff, who will enter his 19th year as leader of the world's Roman Catholics later this month, has repeatedly said he wants to lead the Church into the third millennium and has kept up a punishing schedule despite obvious frailty and fatigue.
